lesson_title: Walk the Queue of One Hundred
hook_text: Line up 100 South Africans by income. Walk past 60 of them. You've counted a tenth of the money.
clip_script: Line up one hundred people from emptiest plate to fullest, and walk down the queue adding up what they hold. In a perfectly equal country, halfway down you would have counted half the food. In ours, you can walk past sixty people and still have counted barely a tenth of it — while the last few in the queue hold half the pot between them. That walk has a name: the Lorenz curve. And the number that scores it, from zero for perfect equality to one for one-person-takes-all, sits near nought comma six five here — about the deepest sag ever measured anywhere on Earth. So the country moves food along the queue: taxes that scoop more from fuller plates, grants landing on the emptiest ones, free basic water and power, a floor under wages, land and ownership reform. Five spoons — and every spoon has a handle: grants need a growing pot; the wage floor reaches only those with work; a field without tools feeds nobody yet. Grow the pot AND move the shares. Anyone arguing only one has half an argument.
visual_style: One hundred simple figures in a line, plates growing from empty to overflowing; a walking counter tallying income share along the queue; the tally drawn as a sagging curve beneath a straight diagonal; five spoons moving food backward along the line.
mood: Grave but constructive — the numbers land hard, the tools answer them.
pacing: Measured walk down the queue, a beat of silence at the tenth-of-the-money reveal, brisk through the five spoons, resolute close.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision sweep: the pot, the report card, the one-world shop and the seed mealies.
